stories.title: Measures on childcare, energy costs expected in Budget
stories.summary: The Budget will be announced at 1pm, with the Government promising a personal tax package, measures on childcare and steps to help on energy costs. Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers will announce €8.65 billion in additional Budget spending, consisting of €7bn on new measures and €1.65bn in tax changes. The Cabinet will meet this morning to give the final sign off on the Budget, before Mr Harris and Mr Chambers, in that order, deliver their Budget speeches over 90 minutes in the Dáil chamber. Income-tax proposals will be closely watched after a budget with minimal personal tax changes last year; much to the annoyance of the opposition and some Government backbench TDs. Despite inflation climbing towards 4%, the Government will hope people still feel tax changes in their pockets. This will mark the second Budget since the Fianna Fáil-Fine Gael-Independent coalition came to office in 2025, but is one where fuel prices, the cost of living and the threat of further protests have all shaped the Coalition's political thinking.

stories.title: Teachers to begin work-to-rule tomorrow over pay dispute
stories.summary: Primary and secondary teachers across the country begin a work-to-rule tomorrow morning in a dispute over public sector pay. Members of the Teachers' Union of Ireland (TUI), the Association of Secondary Teachers, Ireland (ASTI) and the Irish National Teachers' Organisation (INTO) voted almost unanimously for the action. The ASTI and INTO's work-to-rule will begin on Monday, 5 October, while TUI members' industrial actions starts a week later on 12 October. The unions say the Government has failed to engage seriously on a new pay deal since the previous public sector agreement expired on 30 June. From tomorrow, teachers will work only their contracted hours. They will not supervise children who arrive early or stay late, and all parent-teacher meetings must take place during school hours. A full strike is planned for Wednesday 14 October, which would close all schools. INTO General Secretary John Boyle said he fully expects it to go ahead, and that a second strike is likely to be approved for 21 October.

stories.title: Bill for Govt hosting EU Presidency rises to over €75m
stories.summary: The bill to the Government is hosting the six-month EU Presidency to the end of August totals €75.2 million. That is according to new figures provided by the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, Jack Chambers. In the figures provided in a written Dáil reply to Independent Ireland TD Ken O'Flynn , Minister Chambers reveals that the largest spend by any Department to date has been €26.3m by the Dept of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. Ireland commenced hosting the EU Presidency on 1 July, and garda overtime would account for the largest portion of the Department of Justice spend, where Minister Chambers further disclosed that the Dept of Foreign Affairs spend on the EU Presidency to the end of August was €20.3m. The bulk of the spend has been made by the two Government Departments along with the Office of Public Works (OPW), which has spent €19.6m on the EU Presidency to the end of August. In his written Dáil reply, Minister Chambers stated that revised Government Estimates 2026 allocated €300m to cover the costs of hosting the EU Presidency.

stories.title: What happens to all the heat generated by Irish data centres?
stories.summary: Analysis: The energy from data centres ultimately becomes heat, but the question is how much of this ends up in somebody's radiator Ireland has spent years debating how much electricity data centres use, their impact on the grid and the infrastructure they require. But far less attention has been paid to what comes out: heat. In 2025, Ireland's data centres used 23% of all electricity metered in the country, up from 5% a decade earlier. That one number has dominated the public debate, but almost every unit of that electricity comes back out as heat. What we do with that heat is a question Ireland has barely started to ask. Inside a data centre, most of the electricity is used by the servers. The rest goes to power conversion, backup systems and the cooling plant: the fans, pumps, chillers and cooling towers that move heat away from the processors. Engineers measure this with a ratio called power usage effectiveness, or PUE: how much extra electricity the building needs beyond the computing itself. A PUE of 1.0 would mean nothing at all goes on overheads. Averaged over a year, the best modern facilities come close to that, while older halls can spend considerably more on overheads. Very little of this is published for individual sites, so it is hard to tell which facilities are efficient. That is beginning to change with EU rules now requiring larger data centres to report their energy use and environmental impact every year. Reporting will not save a single kilowatt-hour by itself, but it is hard to improve something nobody measures. Ireland's climate is an advantage here. For much of the year, outside air is cool enough to remove that heat without much mechanical refrigeration. Warm weather changes the equation: as outdoor temperatures rise, more energy is needed to move the same amount of heat. There is still not enough operational data to say how much extra electricity individual sites use in warm spells.

stories.title: German, US scientists win Nobel prize for optogenetics
stories.summary: American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have won the 2026 ⁠Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discoveries on light and optogenetics that have helped understand how the brain works. The Nobel Assembly of Sweden's Karolinska Institute medical university said Mr Deisseroth, 54, Mr Hegemann, 71, and Mr Nagel, 73, were selected for their "discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics." Optogenetics "makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain," said Thomas Perlmann, Secretary-General of the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet. "This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain's mysteries," Mr Perlmann said. In clinical trials, researchers are restoring vision to people blinded by a condition called retinitis pigmentosa by inserting a light-sensitive protein in the retina. Researchers also hope optogenetics could improve cochlear implants, allowing more precise stimulation of the auditory nerve than current electrical devices.

stories.title: Frawley and O'Shea adding greater lust to out-half debate
stories.summary: It was a tale of two Irish out-halves in last weekend's United Rugby Championship matches. Ciarán Frawley made the best first impression possible at his new club, guiding Connacht to victory over Benetton in Italy with a late try to seal the win. It is a dream start for the former Leinster utility back who has made the less conventional move west to prove a point to many people, including the Irish coaches and his former mentors at Leinster. Frawley is a talented footballer. It’s the reason he got caught in the dreaded utility role. He was so good at covering multiple positions that he never quite nailed down a sustained opportunity to make the number 10 jersey his own. When he did get his chance to perform in his preferred jersey, he had some sublime moments, mixed with some periods where he under performed. It’s not surprising that when a player in a key position fails to get enough game-time in a game management position, he fails to perform to the required level on the international stage. Though it didn’t stop him from converting a pair of memorable drop goals to beat South Africa in their own back yard. Frawley has a sizeable frame. It’s the reason why he can perform at centre and full-back. His size allows him to be a real attacking threat, taking the ball as close to the tackle line as any of the best Irish attacking out-halves. His decision making in traffic is helped by his ability to manage himself in contact. When he’s confident, there’s venom in his attacking style.

stories.title: GAA round-up: All-Ireland champions fall
stories.summary: A number of county and provincial champions - as well as All-Ireland holders Daingean Uí Chúis - surrendered their titles as the club season continued to heat up around the country. All-Ireland winners Daingean uí Chúis saw their reign end as they exited the Kerry SFC, losing to Spa 1-17 to 1-11 in their Round 3 clash on Saturday. The Killarney side were full value for their win, with a late goal from Cian Murphy putting the gloss on things. Spa held a four-point advantage at the break - 0-12 to 1-05 - with Cathal Bambury netting for the now deposed champions. Daingean uí Chúis started the second half well and were only a point in arrears with over ten minutes left, thanks a Paul Geaney two-pointer, but they couldn't recover. Elsewhere, David Clifford stood out again as a late orange flag from him saw East Kerry edge Mid Kerry by the bare minimum - 1-12 to 1-11. Sunday's action saw An Ghaeltacht defeat Templenoe 1-14 to 0-15, while North Kerry were too strong for Na Gaeil on a 2-16 to 0-11.

stories.title: LOI great Bolger set to retire from playing
stories.summary: League of Ireland great Greg Bolger has announced he will retire at the end of the season. Bolger won a league title and FAI Cup with three different clubs during his stellar career which lasted nearly two decades. The Wexford man played for UCD, St. Patrick's Athletic, Sligo Rovers, Sporting Fingal, Dundalk, Cork City and Shamrock Rovers. He won a title and cup with the Saints, City and the Hoops, while he won a second cup with Cork during their 2017 double success. The 38-year-old will play his final match in the Rebels' closing home game of the year against Finn Harps on Friday in Turners Cross. They will lift the First Division trophy after the game. In the last three seasons he has helped them to two promotions and captained them in last year’s FAI Cup final defeat to Shamrock Rovers.

stories.title: O'Shea lights up Thomond Park as Munster beat the Bulls
stories.summary: Charlie O'Shea announced himself to Thomond Park with a sensational performance, as the young out-half steered Munster to an impressive bonus-point win against the Bulls in Limerick. The 20-year-old scored two tries and kicked three conversions in his first start for the province, and was given a standing ovation as he departed on 68 minutes following a dazzling performance in Munster’s 26-22 win. His first try was all heart as he charged down a clearance kick from Curwin Bosch before winning a race to the line, before an acrobatic dive to the corner in the second half nudged Munster into a 19-17 lead from which they never looked back. Even before his two tries, the Corkman was catching the eye, sending a stunning crossfield kick to Diarmuid Kilgallen for Munster’s opening try, and drawing a majestic conversion in off the right touchline. Clayton McMillan’s side had to come from 7-0 down early on and trailed 17-14 early in the second half, but they were full value for their bonus-point win as they dominated the final 30 minutes, with O’Shea’s second try and a bonus-point score from Alex Kendellen giving them a much-needed win to kick-start their season, although the head coach will be sweating on more injuries, as Michael Milne (below) limped out in the opening half. The opening minutes were played out largely in the Bulls 22, as two penalties gave Munster the chance to set up camp in opposition territory, although they couldn't make it count as Sean O'Brien's knock-on ended the attack, while an early injury to Michael Milne compounded the frustration.

stories.title: Cinema at the edge of Ireland - Disappear Here returns to Donegal
stories.summary: Set between the mountains and the Atlantic on Donegal's wild Inishowen Peninsula, Disappear Here is a film festival with a difference… Founder and Festival Director Michael McLaughlin tells more ahead of this year's installment, which runs from October 16th - 18th. When I started Disappear Here Film Festival in Ballyliffin in 2017, the idea was to bring films to the north-west that people here might never otherwise get the chance to see. I also wanted filmmakers to experience Donegal as more than a location on a screen, but as a place where their work could find an audience and start a conversation. Our masterclasses and workshops in acting, producing and writing are a big part of that. A screening can inspire someone to make a film and practical support can then help them take the first step. I know how much it matters to be able to learn from working people in the industry, ask honest questions and meet others who are trying to find their way in. We are increasingly seeing filmmakers make Disappear Here an established stop in their festival circuit strategy. For many Irish filmmakers, the festival offers a chance to bring their work to a Donegal audience and connect with fellow filmmakers in an intimate setting. Our international engagement is growing too. It is exciting to see films travel to Ballyliffin from further afield, and to watch audiences here respond to stories they might never have encountered otherwise. When Star Wars: The Last Jedi filmed at Malin Head, it brought international attention to Inishowen's coastline. The Northman later used Five Fingers Strand as a filming location. These and a multitude of other productions showed what Donegal could offer a major film crew. Just as encouraging is the growth of filmmaking within the county, the people developing ideas, building skills and creating work of their own.

stories.title: Gillian Anderson addresses 'distracting' theatre fans
stories.summary: Gillian Anderson has explained why she asked a group of fans not to sit in the front row of her West End show Who's Afraid Of Virginia Woolf?. In a video shared online, the Sex Education star, 58, was seen telling fans outside the Soho Place Theatre: "You guys cannot sit in the front row. "I don’t care; you cannot sit in the front row. It’s so distracting." The fans, who were off camera, can then be heard apologising while Anderson added: "You can’t come 20 times and sit in the front row, it’ll drive me mad." After the video was shared widely on social media, Anderson clarified that she knows the women she was speaking to in the clip. She wrote on X: "The video doing the rounds is me talking with women I go back over 20 years with – so please don’t say anything negative to or about them.

stories.title: 10 easy ways to stretch your budget for the food shop
stories.summary: Sophie Morris from How to Shop Well Now shares her tips and tricks for reducing the price of our groceries. The average household makes 23 trips to the supermarket every month—ranging from the main weekly shop to quick top-ups throughout the week. On How To Shop Well, our goal was to share practical tips for buying great quality food while keeping your weekly bill under control. With the average Irish family of four currently spending €180 a week on groceries, adopting a few simple habits can make a noticeable difference to your budget. Many of these tips sound obvious, but very few of us put all of them into practice consistently. Frozen fruit and vegetables are often better value than fresh, conveniently pre-prepared, and still deliver the same nutritional value. Crucially, opting for frozen virtually eliminates food waste since you only use what you need. Fruit and Veg are the most commonly wasted items in our homes, with 39% of us throwing gone-off produce into the bin. Only 54% of shoppers regularly use a list, yet it is the best tool for staying on budget. Focus on one main weekly shop, and which could eliminate top-up shops, which are usually where impulse spending happens. Before heading out, audit your fridge, freezer and presses. Keep a regular master list of your household staples, and only add new items when old ones run out. Finding real value requires a bit of hunting. Never shop on an empty stomach or when you are rushed. Supermarkets can sometimes place higher-margin items at eye level, so take a moment to look at the top and bottom shelves where the best-value brands and bulk items are usually placed.

stories.title: Larger package of tax measures in Budget than expected
stories.summary: The Budget will include a larger package of tax measures than expected. Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris will announce tax changes of €1.65 billion, which is €150 million more than originally expected due to additional steps to deal with the energy shock. The point at which people pay the higher 40% rate of tax will be increased by €2,500 to €46,500. Personal, employee and earned income tax credits will increase by €125 to €2,125, effectively reducing the liability of earners. As the Government agrees to the recommendation of the Low Wage Commission to increase the minimum wage by 79 cent per hour to €14.94, it will also increase the point at which the 2% rate of Universal Social Charge is paid. Cumulatively, the changes will mean that for a couple with a joint income of €100,000 they would benefit by €1,500 or a single person on €50,000 would benefit by €750.

stories.title: Chief Justice urges end to legal aid dispute
stories.summary: Chief Justice of Ireland Donal O'Donnell has said the continuation of the dispute between criminal defence solicitors and the Department of Justice is a matter of concern to him and to judges generally. Mr Justice O’Donnell was speaking at a ceremony in the Four Courts to mark the beginning of the new legal year. More than 100 solicitors and barristers working in criminal defence walked out of court in Dublin as the new term began to mark their continuing dispute over a new payment scheme for criminal legal aid. The solicitors have been in dispute with Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan since June, when the new structure was introduced. It provided for a flat-fee payment of €520. They were joined on the steps of the Criminal Courts of Justice by barrister colleagues from the Irish Criminal Bar Association. The solicitors say the flat-fee payment does not take into account complicated cases where multiple court appearances may be necessary.

stories.title: Two factors preventing ministers from budget utopia
stories.summary: Rarely has so much cash coalesced with such levels of political angst. These are not the days of austerity when the late Brian Lenihan pledged that swingeing cuts would allow the country to turn the proverbial corner. However, two complicating factors are preventing ministers from entering budget utopia. This first is rising energy costs, followed closely by soaring grocery bills. That presents the seemingly strange scenario where the country is getting richer, but households are watching their disposable income shrink. Obviously, the Budget, which will be unveiled on Tuesday, must leave workers and families feeling that they were helped.

stories.title: Oil gains as traders weigh Gulf tensions against exports
stories.summary: Oil prices made slight gains today as security concerns in the Middle East kept a geopolitical risk premium in the market, even as resilient regional crude exports and a G7 emergency stockpile release eased supply concerns. Brent crude futures were up 27 cents, or 0.3%, at $100.59 a barrel early this morning, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 30 cents, or 0.3%, to $89.73 a barrel. "Shipping data shows regional crude exports actually exceeded pre-war levels on several days in late September. Alternative routes and logistical adjustments have somehow allowed producers to keep barrels moving despite the disruption around Hormuz," said Priyanka Sachdeva, head of market insights at Phillip Nova. "However, calling this a full normalisation of supply doesn't look justified quite yet. There have been renewed attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz, and the number of incidents has increased in recent days. This means that while barrels are still moving, the cost, insurance, routing, and security risks of moving them remain elevated," he said. Gulf oil flows excluding Iran surged to over 81% of pre-war levels in September, data showed, led by a recovery in Saudi exports despite attacks on the kingdom's oil infrastructure and escalating Iranian attacks on regional shipping, while Iranian exports fell to zero due to a US blockade. Further easing supply concerns, G7 countries agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves and pledged to refrain from energy export restrictions after pressure from US President Donald Trump.

stories.title: Crawford's U21s ready for down-to-the-wire scenario
stories.summary: Jim Crawford says Ireland are prepared for every eventuality as they head into this evening's final-day showdown against England (6pm) with a European Under-21 Championship play-off spot on the line. The Boys in Green hold the all-important second spot in Group D, but only a victory over Lee Carsley’s Young Lions, who are already qualified as table-toppers, will guarantee their progression. Failing that, Ireland would require Slovakia to slip up in Andorra. Both sides are tied on 17 points, but Ireland possess the head-to-head tiebreaker. This down-to-the-wire scenario at a sold-out Turner’s Cross looked unlikely after Crawford’s side were humbled 4-0 by the Pyrenean microstate, but three consecutive wins have put them in control of their own destiny. Andorra remain unbeaten at home in this group (two wins, two draws) and were only denied a famous victory over England by a 90th-minute Rico Lewis penalty. Still, Crawford isn’t expecting any favours. "The unfortunate thing is that Andorra, when they played against us, they dropped down quite a few first-team players. I don't think that's going to happen against Slovakia," he said.

stories.title: Rafferty 'immensely proud' as he ends Armagh career
stories.summary: Ethan Rafferty has said he is "immensely proud" of what Armagh have achieved in recent years after becoming the latest Orchard County player to call time on their county career. Earlier this week, it was revealed that former captain Rory Grugan and James Morgan had also retired. Grange man Rafferty first saw the inside of an Armagh dressing room in 2004, acting as waterboy for the county's Under-21s as the side, managed by his father Peter Rafferty, Mattie Lennon and Colm Marley, went on to claim an All-Ireland title. He would go on to represent the county at underage level before being invited into the senior panel by Paul Grimley ahead of the 2013 season. A year later, Kieran McGeeney joined as head coach before stepping up to the manager's position a season later. It was under 'Geezer' that Rafferty - the first Grange man to get his hands on the Sam Maguire as a player - became one of the most high-profile players in the game having been converted from an attacking half-forward to a goalkeeper for the 2022 season.

stories.summary: Portugal boss Jorge Jesus has opened the door for Cristiano Ronaldo to resume his international career. Ronaldo left the national team squad after he was an unused substitute for a 2-1 win away to Norway in the Nations League on 27 September. Five-time Ballon d'Or winner Ronaldo vowed to "tell the truth" in due course in a spat which threatened to end the international career of the Al Nassr forward, who has scored a record-breaking 146 goals in 234 appearances for Portugal. Yet, after Sunday’s 2-1 home win over Norway, Jesus told a press conference: "If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team. "We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who’s going to decide. "In my first call-up, I said, 'I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you’. And now I’m saying the same thing."

stories.title: Bond & Buckley to Baldur's Gate: Irish actors making it in gaming
stories.summary: Whether it's TV, film or theatre, on stage or on screen, the Irish have always punched above their weight, delivering mesmerising performances that continue to set the standard in the entertainment industry. We are a nation of storytellers, after all. And in the world of gaming, that’s still the case. Several Irish actors have become central to some of the best games you can play, captivating us as endearing characters and helping sculpt stories we still think fondly of today. From action and adventure to psychological horror, comedy and more, here’s a quick rundown of some of the best appearances from the Irish you can find on a console. While the film industry drags its heels in deciding who will take on the 007 mantle, Irishman Patrick Gibson is leading the charge on the gaming front, portraying Bond in the brand-new 007 First Light, released earlier this year. The game is an original take on the early parts of Bond's career, and became a critical success upon release, with Gibson’s performance receiving its due acclaim. The actor brings the inexperience of a fledgling agent to the forefront, while still developing his suave, signature silver tongue. With the Game of the Year awards only a few short months away, expect Gibson to be in contention in the performance category. And hopefully, he’ll carry on the mantle of the digital Bond well into the future.

stories.title: Bowie events to mark what would have been 80th birthday
stories.summary: Special events, releases, collaborations, and fan experiences have kicked off around the world to mark what would have been David Bowie's 80th birthday next year. Bowie, widely regarded as one of the greatest artists of all time, would have turned 80 on 8 January next year. He died aged 69 on 10 January, 2016 after an 18-month battle with cancer. A decade on, a celebration of his life and career has been announced. Titled Bowie80, organisers say the events will acknowledge how Bowie's impact can still be "seen, heard, and felt across all forms of art and in mainstream and outsider culture spanning both the 20th and 21st centuries". The events, which start on Monday and will continue throughout next year, will be announced through the bowie80.davidbowie.com website.

Recruitment and efforts to secure additional Special Needs Assistants (SNA) cover will continue. The school said it appreciated the understanding of the school community as they worked to resolve the situation. ''The wellbeing and educational needs of the school's students continue to remain our highest priority," the statement concluded.

stories.title: Bolsonaro leads Lula as Brazil election goes to run-off
stories.summary: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of the far-right former leader Jair Bolsonaro, finished ahead of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil's election, which will go to a run-off in three weeks. In a surprise result that defied opinion poll projections showing Mr Lula in the lead, Flavio Bolsonaro received around 47% of the vote to the incumbent's 45%. If Mr Bolsonaro wins in the 25 October election, Brazil will be the latest country to swing to the right in Latin America, a trend championed by US President Donald Trump. The election also included a series of significant wins for the right in parliament, a setback for Mr Lula, who at 80 is seeking a fourth term in office to cement his legacy. Mr Bolsonaro's Liberal Party, the largest party in the Senate, secured 19 of the 54 seats being contested but fell short of an outright majority. Mr Lula branded the vote a battle between democracy and "barbarism", warning voters that Brazil's sovereignty was at stake in the face of US pressure.

stories.title: UniCredit Russia unit's reorganisation and sale approved
stories.summary: President Vladimir Putin has approved the reorganisation of the Russian subsidiary of Italy's UniCredit and the subsequent sale of the newly created unit, according to a decree published on the Russian government's website. The reorganisation and sale required presidential approval under Russia's restrictions on deals involving assets owned by investors from countries deemed "unfriendly" by Moscow. UniCredit had long been one of the largest Western banks in Russia, along with Austria's Raiffeisen and Hungary's OTP, maintaining operations following the invasion of Ukraine despite pressure from European regulators to exit. The bank said in May it had struck a non-binding deal to sell parts of its Russian bank to a "well-established private investor" in the United Arab Emirates, retaining only its payments business in Russia. It said it would split its Russian business in two and keep full ownership of the payments arm, with the unidentified UAE buyer acquiring the rest. It did not disclose the deal value. stories.title: Gauff hits out at racist abuse after replayed point drama
stories.summary: Coco Gauff said she had received an "insane" amount of racial abuse on social media after the two-times Grand Slam champion beat local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open on Monday in a match where a replayed point sparked an online backlash. The American won 7-5 6-1 to reach the fourth round, but was targeted after stopping play during a crucial point in the first set, raising her hand to complain about a flickering advertising board just as Sun was about to put away a winner. After a video review, the umpire ordered the point to be replayed. Gauff won the replayed point and held serve for 5-5 before cruising to victory against the Chinese 16-year-old. Gauff, 22, said she had received a barrage of abusive messages on social media after the match. "You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff said on X early on Tuesday in reply to a post containing a racial slur. "The amount of racist comments/direct messages I've received in the last few hours is insane.
